title: Volcanoes that made history
gist: Volcanologists reconstruct how sulfur-driven climate shocks from eruptions — Krakatau 1883, Samalas 1257, an unidentified 1345 blast, Laki 1783, Tambora 1815 — cascaded into harvest failures, famines, epidemics, and mass migration. The reusable lesson is that identical climate shocks produce wildly different societal outcomes depending on pre-existing vulnerability and access to trade and transport networks.

themes.theme: Sulfur as the climate transmission mechanism

insights.claim: The climate-driving component of a large eruption is sulfur, which forms aerosols that reflect sunlight and cool Earth for months to years — not the ash or the visible spectacle.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Sulfur output, not eruption size or fatalities, is the variable that predicts downstream agricultural and macro disruption.
insights.quote: Once sulfur erupts into the atmosphere, it can form particles called aerosols that reflect sunlight and cool Earth.

insights.claim: After Krakatau's 1883 eruption, average summer temperatures fell 0.6 degrees Celsius across the non-tropical Northern Hemisphere.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: A sub-one-degree hemispheric cooling was enough to be economically consequential — small climate deltas carry large agricultural leverage.
insights.quote: average summer temperatures fell 0.6° Celsius (1.1° Fahrenheit) in the non-tropical regions of the Northern Hemisphere
insights.locator: In the months and years after the eruption

insights.claim: The 1257 Samalas eruption in Indonesia dwarfed all others in recent history as measured by sulfur output and chilled Northern Hemisphere climate for several years afterward.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Establishes the upper bound of the historical record — a useful benchmark for tail-risk scenarios of a modern eruption.
insights.locator: The 1257 eruption of the Samalas volcano

themes.theme: Forensic tools for dating past eruptions

insights.claim: Polar ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica preserve annual sulfur and ash layers that let researchers read atmospheric history back in time like turning the pages of a book.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Ice cores supply the physical fingerprint that converts historical anecdote into a datable, quantified shock series.
insights.locator: Scientists can infer that big eruptions happened

insights.claim: Tree-ring studies of annual growth layers independently identify which years had good or bad growing weather, providing a second dataset that can corroborate ice-core sulfur signals.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Two independent proxies converging is what makes eruption-to-society causal claims defensible rather than speculative.
insights.locator: Tree-ring studies, which analyze annual growth layers

insights.claim: Ice cores contain large amounts of sulfur dated to 536 CE — matching contemporaneous accounts of an 18-month haze across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia — yet the responsible volcano remains unidentified, possibly in then-unpopulated Iceland.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Major climate-altering eruptions can leave no attributable source at all, which is a hard limit on the completeness of any historical hazard catalog.
insights.locator: It turns out that polar ice cores do contain

insights.claim: It took until 2013 for an interdisciplinary team to radiocarbon-date deposits around Samalas and tie it to the known 1257 sulfur spike, showing how recently the eruption-attribution problem was still open.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: The field's attribution capability is barely a decade old, so historical volcano-society links are still being actively revised.

insights.claim: Büntgen's team used tree rings to confirm unusually cold and wet summers in southern Europe in 1345, 1346, and 1347, then argued that resulting crop failures drove grain imports from farther east whose ships carried rats harboring Yersinia pestis.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: A climate shock propagated into pandemic through the trade response to it, not directly — supply-chain adaptation was itself the vector.
insights.quote: the mystery volcano erupting in 1345 may have set off a chain of events that ultimately killed tens of millions of people

insights.claim: Tree-ring records show extensive cooling across North America and Eurasia from 1257 to 1259 following Samalas, with starvation in England and damaged rice production in Japan from wet, cool summers.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: A single tropical eruption produced simultaneous harvest failures on multiple continents — the correlated-shock scenario that defeats geographic diversification.
insights.locator: Tree-ring studies, which analyze annual growth layers

insights.claim: Some researchers speculate Samalas helped seal the Mongol Empire's fate, which ended after its last ruler died in a 1259 epidemic in China possibly linked to eruption-caused climate change.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Framed as speculation, not proof — a useful reminder that the field distinguishes correlation from regime-collapse causation.

insights.claim: The Laki fissure eruption in Iceland spewed lava for eight months from June 1783 and killed at least one-fifth of Iceland's people and much of its livestock through toxic fog and harvest-ruining climate change.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Local mortality from a fissure eruption can reach 20 percent of a national population — the domestic toll dwarfs the remote climate effect.
insights.locator: The source turns out to be Laki

themes.theme: Trade access as the resilience variable

insights.claim: After Tambora's 1815 eruption, Eastern Europe and western Russia had relatively better growing conditions and grain to export, while port cities like London and Hamburg enjoyed access to imported grain and prices rose sharply in the hinterlands.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: The reusable model: connectivity to trade and transport networks, not the size of the shock, determined who starved — the same logic applies to modern supply-chain positioning.
insights.quote: Those bright spots show how access to transportation and trade networks can make societies more resilient in the face of disaster.
insights.locator: Eastern Europe and western Russia, in contrast

insights.claim: Tambora's cooling produced the 1816 'year without a summer,' bringing famine to Switzerland and Ireland, soaring grain prices and malnutrition in parts of Europe, and prompting tens of thousands to emigrate to North America.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Mass migration was the second-order consequence of a one-year commodity shock — a template for climate-driven population movement.

insights.claim: A Cambridge volcanologist frames outcomes as a collision between shock timing and societal state: some climate shocks pass harmlessly, while others arrive when vulnerabilities are already elevated.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Damage is a function of the interaction between exogenous shock and pre-existing fragility — screen for fragility, not just for hazard exposure.
insights.quote: Some climate shocks will come and go…. At other times, the climate shock will come … when there are greater societal vulnerabilities.
insights.locator: Human society has a lot of susceptibilities

insights.claim: Krakatau in 1883 was the first catastrophic eruption documented globally in near real time thanks to Victorian-era telegraphy, and that documentation laid the foundations for modern volcanology.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: A communications-technology upgrade, not a scientific breakthrough, created an entire scientific discipline — the pattern repeats with each sensing generation.
insights.quote: Where once Mount Krakatau stood the sea now plays.
insights.locator: The first telegram arrived in Singapore

insights.claim: Krakatau's 1883 eruption obliterated two islands and most of a third in the strait between Java and Sumatra, killing more than 36,000 people, the majority in tsunamis rather than the blast itself.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Secondary tsunami effects, not the eruption, drove the casualty count — hazard models weighted to the primary event will understate exposure.

insights.claim: In 1784, Benjamin Franklin, then American ambassador to France, linked the strange haze crossing the European countryside to a distant eruption — an inference contemporaries in a pre-electronic world could not otherwise make.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Attribution latency was measured in years before telecommunications; today it is instant, but the forecasting of consequences still is not.
insights.quote: They wouldn’t get news alerts on their phone, they wouldn’t see livestreams of this eruption — they would have no idea

insights.claim: Researchers treat past eruptions as natural experiments for modern climate response because, although big eruptions cool rather than warm the planet, they represent the same class of rapid planetwide shock societies now face.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Historical eruption case studies are the only empirical dataset on how human systems absorb fast global climate shifts.
insights.locator: These lessons may hold particular relevance today

insights.claim: Volcanologists treat the next major eruption as a matter of when, not if, and argue that only study of past events like Krakatau and Tambora gives any idea of what will follow.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: An under-modeled tail risk to global agriculture and commodity prices with no forecastable timing — a case for structural rather than tactical hedges.
insights.quote: it is only a matter of time before the next big blast
